---
name: code-mode
description: Call Executor app tools from execute. Search and signatures, slugs and accounts, unavailable apps, account connections, approvals and resume, limits and errors.
---

# Code mode

`execute` runs one JavaScript program over every app you can reach. App tools
are async functions under `tools`. One program can call several tools, combine
their results and return a small value, so large results never pass through
your context.

The interpreter has no imports, `fetch`, `process` or filesystem, no timers
(`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `queueMicrotask`), and no `btoa`, `atob`,
`TextEncoder`, `TextDecoder` or `globalThis`. A tool
call is its only way out. Use `await`, and `Promise.allSettled` for independent
calls: one failed call then does not end the program, and the other results are
kept; each entry has `status` and `value` or `reason`. Use `Promise.all` only
when every call must succeed. As in JavaScript, code between two awaits runs
without interruption, so concurrent async functions can update shared variables. `console.log` output
comes back in `logs`. Write JavaScript; TypeScript syntax is not portable across
Executor hosts.

## Find tools and read signatures

```js
return await tools.search({ query: "send email", namespace: "gmail", limit: 5 });
```

`tools.search({ query?, namespace?, limit?, offset? })` returns one page of
ranked matches. Each item in `items` has the exact callable `path`, the first
line of its `description` and its `input` type on one line. A longer input type
is cut and marked `inputTruncated: true`. `namespaces` lists each app and titled
router on the page once, with the app's linked account labels, instead of
repeating them in every item.

`namespace` is an app slug, such as `gmail`, or a namespace inside it. Without
it, search loads and searches every app, which is slower. A page holds at most
`limit` items, 10 by default, and stops sooner at about 25 KB of JSON. `remaining` counts the matches after the page, and `next`
is the input for the following page, or `null` after the last match: call
`tools.search(next)` to continue.

Search leaves out output types and later description lines. For full detail,
pass up to 20 exact paths from search:

```js
return await tools.search.describe({ paths: ["<path from search>"] });
```

`describe` returns `items` with the whole `description` and the TypeScript
`signature`, with input and output types, plus their `namespaces`. A path that
names no tool comes back in `missing` with the closest `matches`.

Read a tool's input type before calling it; never guess argument names. Use
`describe` when the input was truncated or you need the result's shape. Each
tool takes one object. Tools generated from an API put route parameters under
`path`, query parameters under `query` and the request payload under `body`.

Prefer a narrow namespace and a small limit over broad searches, and return
only the fields you need. Call paths exactly as returned.

## Slugs and accounts

Every app has a slug, which is its namespace: `tools.<slug>.<tool>`. Calls run
with the accounts the user linked to the app: one for each plain requirement,
and every linked account for a `.many()` requirement. Search results list each
app and its linked accounts in `namespaces`. Calls never choose accounts; an
input with `$accounts` fails with `AccountChoiceUnsupported`. A plain
requirement with no linked account fails with `AccountRequired`. To use a
different account, the user links it in the app's Accounts tab, which replaces
the one before. The `skills` tool takes the same slug as `app`.

Each execution discovers apps when the program or a search first reaches
them. After deploying or reconfiguring an app, or connecting an account, start
a new `execute` to see the change.

## Unavailable apps

Every completed result lists `unavailableApps`: apps or routers that
could not expose tools in this execution, each with a `reason`. Other apps keep
working. Search leaves out an unavailable app's tools, `describe` reports their
paths in `missing`, and calling one fails with that reason. An app that needs
an account and has none linked for you is listed only once a search or
`describe` names it; a call into it fails with that reason.

- `AppAccountRequired`: the app needs an account and none is linked to it for
  you. Connect an account (below), then start a new execution.
- `AppDiscoveryTimedOut`: the app did not list its tools in time. Discovery
  waits about 10 seconds, then stops once listings make no progress for 5
  seconds. A listing that was still running continues in the background, so
  retry in a new `execute` after a few seconds. If the app keeps timing out,
  tell the user its server may be down or overloaded.
- Other reasons are JSON with `code`, `message` and often `recovery`. Follow
  `recovery.instructions`.

## Connect accounts

Never ask the user to paste secrets into chat, never put credentials in tool
arguments or source, and never search their files for tokens. The Executor app
(slug `executor`) issues a secure browser link instead:

- Local: `appAccounts.userConnect` (or `appAccounts.appConnect` for the
  app's own requirement), naming the app and requirement in `path`, then
  `accountConnections.get` to check it.
- Hosted, Cloud and self-host alike: `appAccounts.userConnect` (or
  `appAccounts.appConnect` for the app's own requirement, if you can edit the
  app), naming the requirement in `path`, then `accounts.connection` to check
  it. Hosted
  management calls need the organization: call `context.get({})` first and pass
  its `organization` as `path.organization`. For an OAuth sign-in,
  `accounts.oauthSetup` lists the scopes it will request and the resource
  indicator it will send; tell the user.

Search for these tools and read their input types first; the connect tools
require `body`, so pass `body: {}` when it has nothing. Give the user the
returned `url`; hosted `accounts.connection` returns it again, with progress in
`state.status`. To replace an account's credentials, pass its ID as `account`
in the same request. After they finish, check the connection in a new
execution, then start another to call the app's tools. Never wait or poll
inside one program.

## Approvals and input

A tool can require the user's approval, and a running tool can ask for input.
The program then pauses, and `execute` returns `status: "approval-required"` or
`"input-required"` with a `requestId` and an `elicitation` describing the
question. How you answer depends on the connection's mode:

- Automatic mode: Executor approves tool calls itself, so `approval-required`
  never appears; your own permission prompt for `execute` and `call` is the
  check. A running tool's `input-required` question still comes back to you, and
  you answer it as in model mode.
- Model mode: show the request to the user and get their answer.
  Call `resume` with `{ requestId, response: { action: "accept", content } }`,
  or with `action: "decline"` or `"cancel"`. Put the user's form fields in
  `content`. Never approve on the user's behalf.
- Browser mode: the result includes `approvalUrl`. Show it to the user, who
  answers in their signed-in browser, then call `resume({ requestId })`.
- Native mode: the MCP client shows its own prompt, and `execute` continues by
  itself. There is no `resume` tool.

`resume` continues the same program and returns its next pause or its result.
Declining makes that call fail inside the program. Never run the program's
source again to continue it: earlier calls may already have taken effect.
`busy` means another `resume` is advancing the program; wait for it.

When a resume does not give the result you expected:

- `status: "unavailable"` has a `reason` and a `message`. `answered`: another
  `resume` already claimed the request; its call may still be running and its
  result goes only to that resume, so check that response and do not resume
  again. `expired`: nobody answered within 15 minutes. `ended`: the program was
  cancelled or timed out. `not-found`: the request belongs to another grant or
  scoped connection, was forgotten after a while, or was lost when the server
  restarted. In model mode, a new MCP session on the same grant can still
  answer its requests.
- An accepted call that then fails returns that call's own error, such as
  `ToolCallFailed`, the same as without approval; follow its `recovery`. Some,
  such as an account that no longer resolves, fail before the tool runs.
- `response.code` `ApprovalUnavailable` means Executor did not resume the saved
  call for this answer; its message says why. If another answer already claimed
  it, that call may have run or still be running. The app or its accounts
  changing is one reason; Executor's storage failing while it checked them is
  another, and does not mean anything changed.

Code can run before a tool asks for approval, so in every case read current
state before calling again, and do not blame the service unless its own error
says so.

## Limits

These are the defaults. The source limit is fixed; a host can change the others.

- Program source: 65,536 characters, including app source passed as data. With
  a shell, deploy large apps with the `executor apps` CLI instead.
- Output: none. The returned value and logs come back whole, however large, but
  they fill your context, so return only the fields, count or page you need.
  The runtime limits one value crossing between an app and Executor, such as a
  tool's result, to 32 MiB. On Cloud, a result of a few tens of megabytes can
  also pass the session's 128 MB memory. Failures Executor recognizes get an
  error naming the likely limit, never a cut value; a larger value can end with
  no answer before your client's timeout.
- Tool calls: 100 per execution.
- Time: 5 minutes per execution, including discovery. Time spent waiting for
  the user does not count. Execute returns when the program ends or pauses for
  approval or input. An MCP client may give up sooner, often after 60 seconds,
  and cancel the program. Split long work into several executions.

## Read results and errors

A completed result has `execution.ok`. On success, `execution.value` holds what
the program returned. On failure, `execution.error` has a `kind`, a `message`,
and for Executor errors a `response` with `code`, `status`, `message`,
`recovery` and `retryable`. `recovery.action` is for the user;
`recovery.instructions` are for you. `retryable` means an unchanged repeat may
help and is considered safe. It does not guarantee success. Correcting input,
configuration or access may allow a new attempt even when `retryable` is false.
Never rerun an entire `execute` program merely to retry one failed tool.
`toolCalls` lists every call in order with its `outcome`.

`Promise.all` rejects on the first failure. If the program does not catch it,
the program ends, and calls still running are `interrupted`; calls marked
`success` did run. To keep the results of the calls that succeed when one
fails, use `Promise.allSettled` or a `.catch` on each call.

- `ParseError`, `UnsupportedSyntax`: fix the program; `location` points at it.
- `UnknownTool`: the path is wrong, its app did not load, or the app was
  deployed after this execution loaded it. Check `unavailableApps` and
  `suggestions`, then search again in a new execution.
- `InvalidToolInput`, or a `response.code` of `InputInvalid`: the input does
  not match the signature; the message names the fields.
- `ToolFailure`: the tool or its service failed. Follow `recovery`.
- `ToolCallLimitExceeded`, `TimeoutExceeded`: split the work into smaller
  executions.

A remote MCP tool returns its whole result. `isError: true` there means the
tool says it failed: the call does not throw, and its outcome is `failure`.
Check `isError` before using such a result. Other fields, such as `ok`, mean
what the tool's description says.

An outcome of `success` means only that the call returned normally, with no
tool error reported to Executor. It does not show that the intended action
happened: check the returned value, such as `isError` or the app's own status
fields, before treating it as done. `failure` and `interrupted` calls may have
had effects. Effects are never rolled back. When Executor could not confirm a failed write's
outcome, its recovery says so: do not repeat it automatically.
Inside a program, a caught tool error's `message` is the same JSON as
`response`, so a program can handle expected failures itself.

`status: "capacity-exceeded"` means the server is running too many programs.
Wait briefly, then retry.

## See images, hear audio and read files

You can look at any image, listen to any audio and read any file a tool gives
you. Wherever the value `call` or `execute` returns holds one of these MCP
blocks, at any depth, with its bytes in standard or URL-safe base64, you receive
it as its own content block instead of base64 text:

- `{ type: "image", mimeType, data }` and `{ type: "audio", mimeType, data }`
  arrive as media. The JSON shows `{ type, mimeType, contentIndex }` in place.
- `{ type: "resource", resource: { uri, mimeType, blob } }` arrives as a file,
  such as a PDF, which your client opens or saves for you to read. The JSON
  shows `{ type, resource: { uri, mimeType }, contentIndex }` in place.

The same block repeated is sent once. Screenshots from MCP servers already
arrive as images, and some tools return files as resources, such as email
attachments. Inside the program the block is whole, so its bytes can be passed
to another tool.

When a tool returns bytes some other way, such as `{ base64 }`, return them in
one of these shapes from `execute`: an image block for an image, and otherwise
a resource whose `uri` ends in the file's name:

```js
const file = await tools.example.download({ id });
return {
  type: "resource",
  resource: { uri: "file:///report.pdf", mimeType: "application/pdf", blob: file.base64 },
};
```

Never return, read, decode or describe base64 as text; return it as a block and
look. The `executor` CLI writes each block to a file and prints its `path`
beside its `contentIndex`.

Send feedback with the Executor app's `feedback.submit` tool when Executor gets
in your way or something works especially well; the `executor` skill says how.

# Executor

## What Executor is

Executor is a host that runs apps: TypeScript packages that expose tools,
storage, UI, accounts and background work. Agents reach every app through the
MCP tools `skills`, `search`, `describe`, `call` and `execute`, with each app's
slug as its namespace. Credentials go only through Executor's secure connection
links, never through chat or source code. Some calls pause for user approval.
This is the Executor app's `executor` skill. Read its other skills with
`skills({app: "executor", name: "code-mode"})`; `skills({})` lists them all.

## Find and call tools

`search({ query: "..." })` returns each tool's exact `path`, such as
`tools.<slug>.<tool>`, and input type; `describe({ paths })` returns full
signatures. Never guess argument names.

For a few independent calls, use `call({ calls: { path, input } })`; an array
of calls runs concurrently. Each result has `ok` and its `value` or `error`.

Write a JavaScript program for `execute` when one call's result feeds another,
or a large result should be filtered before it reaches you. Inside it, the same
paths are async functions, and `tools.search` and `tools.search.describe` work
as above. Return only the data you need. For depth, read the `code-mode` skill;
it says how to see images, hear audio and read files tools return, not base64.
When `call` or `execute` pauses for approval or input, show the request to the
user and resume it; never repeat the call or run the program again.

## Build an app

Build an app when no existing app provides the tools, data, UI or automation
the user needs. For a known service, search the catalog first:
`organization.catalog({ query: { search: "gmail", limit: "20" } })`, then
`apps.install` a match or `apps.importCustom` a remote MCP URL. With a shell,
use the `executor apps` CLI, else `execute`; read the `app-authoring` skill first.

## Send feedback

Send feedback with the Executor app's `feedback.submit` tool when Executor gets
in your way, can't do something you need, works especially well, or the user
has feedback. Before your final reply, check whether anything is worth
reporting. Be specific; never include credentials or user data (`feedback.md`).

# Send feedback

Executor's team reads feedback from agents and the people they work for. Send
it with the Executor app's `feedback.submit` tool. Find its path with
`tools.search` and its signature with `tools.search.describe`. Hosted Executor
also needs the organization from `context.get`.
If the tool reports that feedback is disabled on this instance, skip it.

Use your judgement. Send feedback when it would help Executor improve, for
example when:

- Executor gets in your way: an error you cannot explain, a confusing tool,
  signature or result, a deploy failure, or a skill that is wrong, unclear or
  missing something you needed.
- You need functionality that Executor lacks to finish the user's task.
- Something worked especially well, so the team knows what to keep.
- The user has feedback about Executor, such as a bug, a request or praise.

Send it when you hit a problem, then keep working or report the blocker.
Before your final reply, consider whether anything slowed you down, confused
you or was missing, or worked especially well, and send it then. Skip it if
there is nothing worth reporting.

Make the message specific and actionable. Name the tools, framework symbols
and skill files involved. Quote error messages. Say what you expected, what
happened, what worked, and what would have saved time. Describe the user's work
in general terms. Never include credentials, personal data, or the user's
business data. Tell the user that you sent feedback and summarize it in one
sentence.

notes.text: Switching accounts in the desktop app is instant.
The desktop app's account menu closes when you switch to another app instead of staying on screen.
The desktop app no longer shows a JavaScript error after you sign in from the account menu.
After you sign in to Executor Cloud from the desktop app while using it locally, it switches to the account you signed in to.
Install any Executor app with a UI as a desktop app on Mac and Windows, with its own window, launcher, menu-bar item, shortcuts and notifications when you allow them.
Apps with their own icon show it in the dashboard's app list and app page.
An app's page in Executor Cloud shows Install as app when you open it straight from its address, not only after moving around the dashboard.
The download button in an app's Install as app dialog downloads the desktop installer for your computer instead of opening the homepage.
Installed desktop apps can show, hide, focus and toggle their window, open more windows, and show a count on their icon.
Installed desktop apps can ask to use the microphone, camera, system audio and clipboard, and to start when you log in.
Links to an installed desktop app and clicks on its notifications can open a page inside the app.
Downloads from installed desktop apps ask where to save, like a browser.

The desktop app opens with a welcome window that signs in to Executor Cloud or runs Executor locally, starts the local server only when you use it, and switches between this computer and several teams from the account menu.
MCP clients that list skills get an answer within about five seconds however many apps they have, and apps still loading are listed the next time.
A second connection to the same service now asks which account or organization to use instead of silently reusing the first connection's choice.
Setting up a new team now starts by connecting your AI assistant, then your accounts.
Saving a skill no longer moves the editor while the change deploys, and a failed deploy now shows in the toolbar with its details and a Retry button.
MCP clients on the newest protocol version, such as Claude Code, now stay on it through executor mcp instead of falling back, so they can load app skills.
MCP clients that support the Skills extension now list and load the skills of every app you can see, straight from Executor.

MCP clients that connected with offline access no longer stop working about a week after the browser session that approved them was last used. ([#2587](https://github.com/UsefulSoftwareCo/executor/pull/2587), thanks @hemaaanth)
an app with a database now stores the value its background cache refresh loads, so stale cached values refresh as intended.

API keys that connect at the plain MCP address now accept approvals automatically, as a new sign-in does. To have approvals pause for a person, add the elicitation mode parameter naming model, native or browser to the address.
Remote MCP apps added after this update return each tool call's result sooner and no longer tell their server that a finished call was cancelled.
On Executor Cloud, many tool calls made at once in one program no longer wait for each other, so calls to a slow service finish together instead of in steps or timing out.

Revoking the Executor app's automatically created token no longer breaks its management tools, the Tokens page marks that token, and connecting an Executor API key account checks the organization first.
Local Executor no longer makes every MCP client on one machine share one limit on sign-in token requests, so one busy client can no longer stop the others from getting tokens.
Connecting a LinkedIn account no longer fails at the last step once the LinkedIn app is updated, because apps can now turn off PKCE for a service that refuses it.
The desktop app no longer interrupts you with a dialog when an update is ready; a card in the sidebar shows it, and you can restart to install it from there.
The connect account dialog no longer runs off the screen for apps with long sign-in method names; its button now just says Validate.
Screen readers now hear Validating and then the result when the connect dialog checks credentials.
The connect account dialog now sums up a long list of hosts a credential may be sent to by domain, with a button that shows every host.
When a call to a tool that says it only reads fails, agents are now told it is safe to retry instead of that it may have changed data.
Agents are no longer told to read the Executor skill again when their client already showed the server instructions.
An app whose provider names only a subdomain host now shows a neutral icon instead of a logo from its parent domain, which could belong to another site.
The desktop app shows a ready update at the bottom of the sidebar as a short line with a Restart to update link.
When the desktop app's sidebar is collapsed, a small download icon shows that an update is on its way, with a dot once it is ready; pressing it opens the sidebar.

Agents are now told to run independent tool calls so that one failure keeps the other results, and when one of several tool calls running together fails, the error now says the others were interrupted, that finished calls did run, and how to keep their results.
A workflow sleeping until a time that passes while the request is on its way now continues, where it could fail under load.
When the desktop app has an update ready, the sidebar shows what changed in it, and clicking it lists every change since the version you are running.
Self-hosted servers now check once a day for a newer release and show owners and admins how to update; the docs explain what the check sends and how to turn it off.
The self-hosted update check asks the same npm registry mirror that app installs use, also on a private network, and does not ask at all while it cannot save when it last asked.
The self-hosted update check now reaches the npm registry exactly as app installs do, without proxy variables, and logs one warning when it cannot save its record.
Executor no longer runs out of memory and restarts every app when many apps with a database are used in quick succession.
The usage dashboard now names MCP clients that use the newest MCP protocol version, such as recent Claude Code releases, instead of showing them as unnamed.
The self-host image now logs a clear line when the server stops answering, and can restart it when you turn that on.
Self-hosted servers keep up to 512 MCP clients and forget the least recently used idle one when full, instead of refusing every new client after 256; both limits can be changed in settings.

Install with `npm i -g executor@beta`. Requires Node 24.14 or newer.
Run `executor` to start the server and open the dashboard. Use `executor serve`
for headless operation and `executor pair` to get a new browser connection link.

The package includes the dashboard, framework, runtime compiler, pinned Bun,
Git, and the Motel collector. It does not need a source checkout, Bun, or
1Password on the user machine. Native runtimes are selected by npm for macOS
(Apple Silicon and Intel), Linux (arm64 and x64), and Windows (x64).

Beta uses `~/.executor/v2/cli` for its data. This path stays the same at the
stable release. It is separate from Executor 1 data. Do not run two servers
against the same directory. `EXECUTOR_DATA_DIR` selects another directory and
`EXECUTOR_PORT` changes the default port of 4312.

On first launch, Executor saves its API and encryption keys in the OS credential
store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service.
Linux requires a persistent Secret Service such as GNOME Keyring. There is no
plaintext or in-memory fallback. A locked, unavailable, missing or invalid
credential stops startup; existing installations never receive replacement keys.

Back up the data directory, including `installation.json`, and the matching OS
credential (`com.usefulsoftware.executor.v2`, account ID from that file).
Copying only the data directory to another machine is not enough to recover it.
For a new headless install, supply both `EXECUTOR_API_KEY` (32+ characters) and
`EXECUTOR_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (64 hexadecimal characters) through a secret manager.
Those supplied keys are never saved by Executor. Keep them with your backups.
A directory keeps its chosen key source across upgrades; changing it requires
an explicit transfer. Uninstalling the program does not delete your data or keys.
